ui._comment: English source. Keys never change; translate the values. {name} placeholders are filled in by the app; keep them. Keys ending in _html may contain simple HTML tags such as <em>.
ui.brand.tagline: A card game for scientists. Read the research problem, then pick the study design that can actually answer it.
ui.lang.label: Language
ui.footer: Methodical v{version}. The answer key has three tiers because methodologists disagree. Argue with it, and improve it.
ui.home.title_html: Match your research method to the challenge.
ui.home.lede: Read the research problem, play the study design that can answer it, then defend it when Reviewer 2 attacks.
ui.home.play.text: One question at a time: pick the right design from four choices, then defend it in a peer-review round. Filter by suit and difficulty.
ui.home.decks.text: Every Question, Design, Threat, Safeguard, Twist and Programme card, with answers and real historical examples.
ui.quick.title: Can you pick the right design?
ui.quick.text: Flip the card, read the problem and its constraints, then choose.
ui.tip.questions: Research problems from real fields. Each has a suit (the kind of knowledge wanted) and constraints (the situation). Your job: find the design that can answer it.
ui.tip.designs: Study designs, colour-coded by family. Each card shows what it answers, which situations it fits or struggles with, and the biases it is weak against.
ui.tip.threats: Biases and validity threats: the “fallacy” deck. A reviewer plays one against a design that is weak to it.
ui.tip.safeguards: Design and analysis features that counter specific threats: the “refutation” deck. Authors play them to defend their design.
ui.tip.twists: Mid-round surprises such as “Funding cut” that add a constraint and force you to rethink your design.
ui.tip.programs: Cooperative five-stage challenges: one research project, from the first question to the final synthesis.
ui.play.tap_hint: Tap a card to read it full size, then pick it.
ui.play.step1: What kind of knowledge is wanted?
ui.play.step2: They usually decide between otherwise good designs.
ui.play.step3: You'll have to defend your choice against the problem's biggest threat.
ui.verdict.unlisted: Unlisted. At a table you could appeal
ui.review.label: Peer review
ui.ref.title: Key reference: {cite}
ui.card.question: {suit} question
ui.card.appeal: {unlisted}, or +{appeal} if the table upholds your appeal
ui.print.title: {game}: print and play
ui.print.intro: {tagline} Version {version}. {total} cards in standard poker size (63 × 88 mm), 9 per A4 page, plus {mats} research-programme mats (A6, 2 per page).
ui.print.printing_html: Printing. Print at 100% / actual size with background graphics on. Cut along the card edges. All cards share one back (backs.html): print it on the reverse of each sheet, or skip it and use opaque card sleeves, the easiest way to make a print-and-play deck shuffle like a real one.
ui.print.answers_html: Answers are in the separate answer-key booklet (answer-key.html), so the top card of a face-down deck never gives its answer away.
ui.print.key_intro: 🥇 best +3 · 🥈 defensible +1 · ⚠️ trap −2 · unlisted 0 (appeal for +1). Read the why aloud: that is where the learning happens.
